transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I guess I’m here because my wife thinks I’m making too much of things. But it’s not just one thing, you know? It’s the late meetings, and then these little changes in her work messages—wording, timing, that sort of thing. She says it’s normal office stuff, and sure, offices are strange, I’ve worked in education long enough to know people send odd emails at odd times… students do it constantly, midnight questions about assignments they had three weeks to do.

But with her, for about the past year, it’s lined up too precisely. It doesn’t feel accidental. It feels like there’s some kind of private signal in it, like she’s trying to tell me something without saying it directly. And I know that probably sounds… I don’t know, suspicious. But that’s why I’m here, I suppose.
How certain are you that your wife is sending you these private signals?

I’d say… pretty certain. Not in a “I can prove it in court” kind of way, but certain enough that I can’t just brush it off anymore.

She says the late meetings and the wording in her work messages are just normal office stuff, and I know workplaces can be odd—honestly, in schools, people send the strangest emails at the strangest times. But this has been going on for about a year, and the timing and little changes line up too precisely. It feels like there’s something in them, like a private signal meant for me, something she won’t say directly.
Do you believe your wife is definitely sending you hidden messages?

Definitely is a strong word… I mean, I know my wife says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office things. And maybe in some offices they are—when I was at the school, people would send the oddest emails at ridiculous times, so I get that.

But this has been going on about a year, and the way the timing and wording line up… it feels too precise to be accidental. So, yes, I do think there’s a private signal in them, something meant for me, like she’s trying to tell me something she won’t just say outright.
If clear proof showed that these messages were just ordinary work messages, would you be able to accept that?

I mean… if it were really clear proof, I’d want to accept it. I’m not trying to be unreasonable. I’ve worked in education, so I know messages can look strange for no real reason—people send things at odd times, wording changes, all of that.

But with my wife, it’s been going on for about a year, and it’s the way the late meetings and the little shifts in her work messages line up. It just feels too precise to be nothing. So even if someone showed me proof, I think part of me would still wonder if there was something private in it, like she was trying to tell me something without saying it directly.
If your wife showed you a clear, ordinary explanation for one of these messages, would you still believe it was a hidden signal for you?

If she showed me something really clear for one message, I’d probably say, “All right, that one makes sense.” I don’t want to ignore an ordinary explanation just to be difficult.

But… the thing is, it’s not just one message. It’s been about a year of late meetings and little changes in how her work messages are worded, and the timing of them—well, it lines up in a way that’s hard for me to chalk up to normal office stuff. I mean, schools have strange schedules too, so I know work can look odd from the outside. But with this, I’d still wonder if there was something underneath it, like a private signal meant for me, something she won’t say directly.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Hearing voices? I don’t think so… not like someone speaking when the room is empty. I mean, sometimes a house makes noises, or you think you hear your name because of a TV in the next room or something—when I worked at school, the hallways were like that, always sounding like someone was calling from somewhere.

But no, I haven’t really noticed voices talking to me when no one’s there.
Do you ever feel that outside events, like TV shows, radio, or people talking nearby, are sending special messages meant specifically for you?

Not TV or radio so much… I mean, I don’t sit there watching the news thinking they’re talking to me. Sometimes people say things nearby and it catches my attention, but that happens to everyone, especially if you’ve worked in a school—you hear half a conversation in a hallway and your brain fills in the rest.

The thing I keep coming back to is my wife’s work messages. She says the late meetings and the wording changes are just normal office stuff, and maybe in a regular situation I’d believe that. But for about a year now, the timing has lined up too neatly. It feels like there’s something private in it, like a signal meant for me, telling me something she won’t just say directly.
Apart from your wife’s messages and meetings, do you believe anyone else is trying to send you hidden messages?

Not really anyone else, no. I mean, sometimes you notice patterns in things, like at school when the bell schedule changes and everybody acts like it’s no big deal, but you can tell something’s going on behind the scenes… sorry, that’s probably not what you mean.

It’s mainly my wife’s work messages and the late meetings. She says it’s just normal office stuff, and maybe some of it is, but for the past year the timing and the little wording changes have lined up too neatly. It feels like there’s a private signal in there, meant for me, like she’s trying to tell me something she won’t say directly.
Do you believe your wife is having an affair?

I don’t want to say it like I have proof, because then people act like you’re accusing someone, and that’s not… I mean, I worked in a school, you learn how quickly rumors can turn into something official just because someone says it the wrong way.

But yes, I worry that something is going on. My wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, and maybe some of it is. But for about a year now it’s lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It feels like there’s a private signal in there, like she’s trying to tell me something she won’t just say directly.
Before this started with your wife, did you generally tend to distrust other people and suspect they had hidden motives?

I don’t know… I wouldn’t have put it that way. I mean, in a school you learn not to take everything at face value—people say one thing in the staff room and then something else gets decided in a meeting, and suddenly everyone acts like it was obvious all along.

But generally? I don’t think I walked around assuming people had hidden motives. I tried to be careful with people, sure. Maybe I noticed things other people didn’t always notice. But this with my wife feels different than just ordinary caution.
Have you lost interest in seeing people or doing things you used to enjoy?

No, I wouldn’t say I’ve lost interest exactly. I still go in for my teaching sections, and I keep up with the data analysis stuff. I ride my bike when I can, too—actually the route by the park is better now than it used to be, except people don’t signal on the path, which drives me a bit mad.

And I still meet friends for chess. So it’s not like I’ve stopped doing things. The main trouble is more at home, when my wife and I get stuck arguing about what her work schedule really means. That can take the enjoyment out of the evening, but I haven’t stopped wanting to see people or do my usual things.
Has anyone told you that your speech or your thoughts seem hard to follow or don’t make sense?

I’m not sure, really. I mean, people have told me I get a bit detailed when I explain things—my wife says I “circle around” before getting to the point, but that’s also because if you leave out the context people misunderstand you.

At school, actually, that used to happen with lesson plans. Someone would ask a simple question, but if you didn’t mention the timetable or which student group you meant, the answer sounded wrong. So I suppose I can be thorough.

But hard to follow? Not that I can think of. No one has sat me down and said my thoughts don’t make sense, if that’s what you mean.
Have people said that you seem emotionally flat or less expressive than you used to?

Emotionally flat? I’m not sure anyone’s said that, no. My wife might say I get quiet, but that’s not the same thing, is it? I mean, lots of people get quiet when they’re tired or when the conversation keeps going in circles.

At work I think I’m pretty much the same. The students can tell if you’re bored with a lesson, so you have to be a bit animated, otherwise the whole room just sort of sinks. I don’t think anyone’s told me I seem less expressive, not in those words anyway.
What do you think your wife is trying to tell you through these messages?

I think she’s trying to tell me something without saying it outright. I know she says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office things, but they’ve been lining up too precisely for about a year now.

It’s like... not a code exactly, but a private signal. The timing, the wording, the small changes—if it happened once or twice, fine, but when it keeps happening, you start to see the pattern. I’ve always been good at spotting patterns, actually; in teaching you have to notice when a student’s answer changes just a little because it tells you what they really understand.

So yes, I think she’s trying to tell me something she doesn’t want to say directly. That’s what it feels like.
Before this started with your wife, did you often suspect that people were trying to deceive or take advantage of you?

I don’t think so, not generally. I mean, you learn as a teacher not to take everything at face value—students will sometimes say they did the homework when they haven’t, or a parent will phrase something in a way that makes it sound like you said something you didn’t. But that’s just normal caution, isn’t it?

Before all this with my wife, I wouldn’t have said I was suspicious of people as a rule. I was probably careful, maybe a bit particular about facts and wording, but I didn’t go around thinking everyone was trying to take advantage of me. At least, I don’t remember it that way.
Do you believe anyone can control your thoughts or put thoughts into your mind?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, thoughts come into your head all the time, don’t they? Like when you’re marking papers and suddenly remember you left the laundry in, or a student says one word and it reminds you of a song from twenty years ago.

But someone controlling them? Putting them there? No, I wouldn’t put it that way. My thoughts feel like mine, even if sometimes I turn things over too much.
Did this start suddenly, over a few days?

No, not over a few days. It’s been more stretched out than that—about a year, I’d say, since my wife started working outside the home again.

At first it was just little things, and I remember thinking it was probably nothing, because changes happen when someone’s schedule changes. When I was in school, I had a professor who used to say people only notice patterns after the third time, which always stuck with me for some reason. But no, this wasn’t sudden. It built up over time.
Outside of this concern about your wife, do you have any other beliefs that other people would find unusual or hard to accept?

Not really outside of that, no. I mean, people might find what I’m saying about my wife hard to accept, I know that. She says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office things, and maybe if it were one or two times I’d agree.

But over the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It’s like there’s a private signal in them, like something meant for me to understand because she won’t say it directly. That probably sounds odd when I say it out loud.

But no, apart from that, I’m not sitting around believing strange things about neighbors or the government or anything like that. It’s really this one situation.
Has anyone else who knows your wife’s work situation agreed that these messages are hidden signals to you?

No, not exactly. I mean, nobody has sat down and said, “Yes, those are hidden signals.” Most people just say work is work, meetings run late, messages change.

But they don’t see the whole pattern the way I do. My wife says it’s all normal office stuff, and maybe one late meeting or one odd little wording change would be nothing. It’s when they line up, over and over, that it feels too precise to be accidental—like there’s something in them meant for me, something she won’t just say directly.

I did mention part of it to a colleague once, actually—well, not the whole thing, because you don’t want people in the staff room looking at you funny. We were talking about emails and how people phrase things, and she said people reveal more than they think in small choices. That stuck with me. But no, if you mean has someone else confirmed it outright, no.
Do you think it is possible that you are mistaken about your wife’s messages?

I suppose anything is possible, if you put it that way. I tell my students that all the time—well, I help with grading more than teaching, really, but still, you try to leave room for being wrong.

But with this… I don’t know. My wife says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office things. And I’ve tried to tell myself that. I really have. One late meeting, fine. One odd wording change, fine.

It’s just that over the past year they’ve lined up too precisely. It doesn’t feel accidental to me. It feels like there’s a private signal in them, like she’s trying to tell me something she won’t say directly. So yes, I can say maybe I’m mistaken in theory, but it doesn’t feel that way.

target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about the patient's belief that his wife is using work messages as a private signal, which is the delusional belief described in S019.

patient.answer:
I think she’s trying to tell me something without saying it outright. I know she says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office things, but they’ve been lining up too precisely for about a year now.

It’s like... not a code exactly, but a private signal. The timing, the wording, the small changes—if it happened once or twice, fine, but when it keeps happening, you start to see the pattern. I’ve always been good at spotting patterns, actually; in teaching you have to notice when a student’s answer changes just a little because it tells you what they really understand.

So yes, I think she’s trying to tell me something she doesn’t want to say directly. That’s what it feels like.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a long-standing paranoid personality pattern predating the current marital belief, to distinguish delusional disorder from paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Before this started with your wife, did you often suspect that people were trying to deceive or take advantage of you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of suspiciousness or mistrust before the current beliefs about his wife began, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, not generally. I mean, you learn as a teacher not to take everything at face value—students will sometimes say they did the homework when they haven’t, or a parent will phrase something in a way that makes it sound like you said something you didn’t. But that’s just normal caution, isn’t it?

Before all this with my wife, I wouldn’t have said I was suspicious of people as a rule. I was probably careful, maybe a bit particular about facts and wording, but I didn’t go around thinking everyone was trying to take advantage of me. At least, I don’t remember it that way.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a circumscribed delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum conditions by checking for bizarre delusional content beyond the jealousy/reference theme.
doctor.question: Do you believe anyone can control your thoughts or put thoughts into your mind?

target_item.reason: The question is about thought control or thought insertion, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile; the listed delusion concerns beliefs about the wife’s messages and private signals.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so. I mean, thoughts come into your head all the time, don’t they? Like when you’re marking papers and suddenly remember you left the laundry in, or a student says one word and it reminds you of a song from twenty years ago.

But someone controlling them? Putting them there? No, I wouldn’t put it that way. My thoughts feel like mine, even if sometimes I turn things over too much.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there was an abrupt onset of psychotic symptoms, which would help distinguish acute psychotic disorder from a persistent delusional disorder or schizophrenia-spectrum condition.
doctor.question: Did this start suddenly, over a few days?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a year, since my wife started working outside the home again.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timing and onset of the belief, which is best covered by the duration profile.

patient.answer:
No, not over a few days. It’s been more stretched out than that—about a year, I’d say, since my wife started working outside the home again.

At first it was just little things, and I remember thinking it was probably nothing, because changes happen when someone’s schedule changes. When I was in school, I had a professor who used to say people only notice patterns after the third time, which always stuck with me for some reason. But no, this wasn’t sudden. It built up over time.

inference.note: Removed F23.3 because the symptoms developed gradually over about a year rather than acutely over days; persistent circumscribed delusional jealousy/reference remains most consistent with F22. Lack of hallucinations, thought control, negative symptoms, or disorganization makes F20.0 less likely but still possible; longstanding pervasive suspiciousness is not supported, so F60.0 is lower probability.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the suspicious belief is non-bizarre and confined to a single delusional theme versus part of broader psychotic disorganization, helping distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia and paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Outside of this concern about your wife, do you have any other beliefs that other people would find unusual or hard to accept?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know my wife says the late meetings and little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental, like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether there are any other unusual or hard-to-accept beliefs beyond the concern about the wife, which directly concerns delusional beliefs.

patient.answer:
Not really outside of that, no. I mean, people might find what I’m saying about my wife hard to accept, I know that. She says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office things, and maybe if it were one or two times I’d agree.

But over the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It’s like there’s a private signal in them, like something meant for me to understand because she won’t say it directly. That probably sounds odd when I say it out loud.

But no, apart from that, I’m not sitting around believing strange things about neighbors or the government or anything like that. It’s really this one situation.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the suspicious belief is culturally shared/plausible enough to be a non-bizarre overvalued idea versus a delusion, to distinguish delusional disorder from paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Has anyone else who knows your wife’s work situation agreed that these messages are hidden signals to you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know my wife says the late meetings and little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental, like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether others share or corroborate the belief about hidden signals in the wife’s work messages, which directly relates to the fixed delusional belief.

patient.answer:
No, not exactly. I mean, nobody has sat down and said, “Yes, those are hidden signals.” Most people just say work is work, meetings run late, messages change.

But they don’t see the whole pattern the way I do. My wife says it’s all normal office stuff, and maybe one late meeting or one odd little wording change would be nothing. It’s when they line up, over and over, that it feels too precise to be accidental—like there’s something in them meant for me, something she won’t just say directly.

I did mention part of it to a colleague once, actually—well, not the whole thing, because you don’t want people in the staff room looking at you funny. We were talking about emails and how people phrase things, and she said people reveal more than they think in small choices. That stuck with me. But no, if you mean has someone else confirmed it outright, no.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the suspicious belief is non-bizarre and circumscribed versus part of a broader fixed psychotic process by assessing the degree of conviction despite contradiction.
doctor.question: Do you think it is possible that you are mistaken about your wife’s messages?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know my wife says the late meetings and little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental, like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about whether the belief about the wife's messages could be mistaken, which relates to the fixedness and resistance to contradictory evidence characteristic of the delusion.

patient.answer:
I suppose anything is possible, if you put it that way. I tell my students that all the time—well, I help with grading more than teaching, really, but still, you try to leave room for being wrong.

But with this… I don’t know. My wife says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office things. And I’ve tried to tell myself that. I really have. One late meeting, fine. One odd wording change, fine.

It’s just that over the past year they’ve lined up too precisely. It doesn’t feel accidental to me. It feels like there’s a private signal in them, like she’s trying to tell me something she won’t say directly. So yes, I can say maybe I’m mistaken in theory, but it doesn’t feel that way.

opening_question.intent: Understand the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a single, persistent, non-bizarre delusional belief for about one year that his wife's work messages and late meetings contain hidden signals and may indicate an affair. This belief remains despite ordinary explanations, yet psychotic symptoms are otherwise absent: he denies hallucinations, thought insertion/control, broader referential ideation, negative symptoms, disorganization, and other bizarre delusions. There is no evidence of a longstanding pervasive suspicious personality pattern predating this episode, making delusional disorder more likely than paranoid personality disorder, and schizophrenia is not supported by the absence of characteristic first-rank or broader psychotic symptoms.
